title: Euclid resolves fifteen exceptionally faint stellar systems
freshness: Euclid Collaboration preprint submitted November 11, 2026; not yet peer reviewed; preferred 15-day search window.
excerpt: A search through Euclid's first major survey release has resolved 15 extremely faint stellar systems into individual stars for the first time. Five are new discoveries, while ten were previously known only as unresolved patches of light.
whyItMatters: The faintest dwarf galaxies preserve clues about how larger galaxies assembled and how dark matter is distributed on small scales. Euclid can now search for these systems with one consistent method from the Milky Way's outskirts to nearby galaxy groups.
whatToExploreNext: How can astronomers distinguish an ultra-faint dwarf galaxy from a globular star cluster when both contain very few visible stars?

sources.label: Euclid Collaboration: Discovery of fifteen resolved low-surface-brightness stellar systems

body:
## Fifteen systems emerge as collections of stars

Euclid has resolved 15 exceptionally faint stellar systems into individual stars for the first time. Five are new discoveries: three lie in the Milky Way's halo and two sit beyond the Local Group. The other ten had appeared in earlier surveys as dim, unresolved smudges and were catalogued as possible dwarf galaxies, but their distances were poorly known.

The result comes from about 1,900 square degrees of the Euclid Wide Survey included in the mission's first major data release. Researchers searched the catalogue for small concentrations of stars whose colours and brightnesses fit the same expected stellar population at a trial distance. This technique, called isochrone filtering, helps a sparse system stand out from unrelated foreground stars and background galaxies.

Resolving stars changes what can be measured. The team estimated distances for all 15 systems and derived sizes, shapes, luminosities, and stellar masses for 14. It also revealed objects spanning a remarkable range of scales, from a barely populated Milky Way companion to dwarf galaxies several million light-years away.

## A system containing only about 40 Suns of stars

Ursa Minor II, one of the new Milky Way halo discoveries, lies about 20 kiloparsecs from us, or roughly 65,000 light-years. Its visible stars add up to an estimated 40 times the Sun's mass. That places it among the least luminous stellar systems known.

Another new object, Eridanus V, is about 165 kiloparsecs away and contains an estimated 550 solar masses in stars. Its size and brightness fall in a region shared by two different kinds of object: globular clusters, which are dense groups of stars, and ultra-faint dwarf galaxies, which can be dominated by dark matter. The present imaging does not determine which category Eridanus V belongs to.

Fornax 7 lies near the tidal boundary of the Fornax dwarf galaxy and may be associated with it. Here too, the word may matters. Position and distance make a connection plausible, but they do not prove that the two objects share an origin.

## Extending the census beyond the Local Group

Twelve of the resolved dwarf galaxies are about 3 to 5.5 megaparsecs away. Ten are candidate members of the M81 group, though membership remains uncertain for some. Three have an average surface brightness near or fainter than 28 magnitudes per square arcsecond within their half-light radii, a regime where very few galaxies had been known at such distances.

These measurements show why Euclid is useful for nearby-galaxy archaeology as well as cosmology. Its sharp, stable images can separate faint stars, while its wide survey observes many environments in the same way. A less biased census of tiny galaxies can test predictions for how galaxies and their dark matter halos formed.

The paper is a preprint intended for an Astronomy & Astrophysics special issue and has not yet completed peer review. Several classifications and group memberships need spectroscopy or deeper imaging. What Euclid measured directly is a set of coherent stellar concentrations and their photometric properties. Whether every concentration is a dwarf galaxy, star cluster, or tidally disturbed remnant remains an interpretation to test.
